doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Sideman humility: Ralph Burns, Neal Hefti and the Pam ending
summary: He says he only stayed out of musicians' way, and that Ralph Burns and Shorty Rogers fixed the ending of Pam without telling him.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Well you’ve had I think a quite remarkable career in that you’ve moved from one kind of music to another with great skill, and I guess you said it earlier in the interview that you helped people, you didn’t get in their way, you made them sound better.

I don’t know if I helped them, I didn’t get in their way, that was the big thing. You know like I guess they could play, but I didn’t think of it like that until now, when you get a little older you hear things, like you just was playing and I wasn’t up to them guys. Well to me, I didn’t have the knowledge — not Flip so much but Flip’s got knowledge about playing — but I mean some of the other guys like Ralph Burns for instance, I worked with Nelson Riddle, I didn’t realize that he was – Neal Hefti was another, Shorty Rodgers, like Shorty Rodgers on “Pam,” him and Ralph Burns put the ending on it.
On “Pam.” Woody had the recording. And they fixed the ending so it would sound like a little ensemble, which they never told me, they just did it. So they liked me.
Well some other people liked you too.
Not as a player, as a guy.
